title: Memento mori, gently
hookLine: remembering death helps us live well
tomorrow: what's the difference between hope and wishful thinking?

cards: Some people keep a chart of their life in tiny squares, one per week, and shade one in each Sunday night. It sounds grim, a countdown on the wall.
The idea is the opposite: seeing the squares makes the week ahead feel precious. The Church has its own version.
On Ash Wednesday, a thumb of ash crosses your forehead, and one of the lines said comes from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return."

teach.b: So the question: does remembering death make life smaller, or bigger? The Catholic answer is bigger.

Sirach puts it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." Not to scare you; to sort you. Remember the end, and the grudge you're keeping shrinks.
The Latin is memento mori: remember you will die. Saint Benedict, among his tools for good works, tells his monks to keep death daily before their eyes.

Some paintings of Saint Jerome put a skull on his desk, next to his books. And for Catholics the end isn't a wall. The raised body, heaven, the saints: remembering death is remembering where you're going.
Here's something a neighbor tradition shares.
The Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here; but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once."
Two traditions, one discovery: remembering death makes people gentler. And one honest difference.
The Dhammapada's frame is impermanence: all things pass, and seeing that clearly frees you. The Catholic frame is a God who raises the dead. Same habit, different horizon.

how: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with words from Genesis, pray for a good death, and some keep a memento mori, such as a small skull or cross, as a reminder.

o: remember that you will die, so you live well
a Latin blessing said over the graves of saints
a gloomy saying to frighten sinners into church

games.q: the habit, then and now — tap the pairs.
p: quarrels cease when you know the end

s: memento mori is meant to make people afraid
Sirach says it sorts you: remember your last end, and you'll live better.
a Buddhist scripture also links remembering death with peace
the Dhammapada: those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
Catholics and Buddhists understand death in exactly the same way
the habit is shared; the frame differs: impermanence, or a God who raises the dead.

games.q: you and your sister have been fighting all week over a borrowed sweater. you remember memento mori. what does it suggest?
o: let the sweater go; the end makes the fight look small.
win the fight first, then be gentle, since life is short.
stop speaking to her; life's too short for drama.
games.why: remembering the end shrinks quarrels. Sirach and the Dhammapada agree on that much.

practice: Choose the next hour of your day. Name the one thing most likely to steal it: the scroll, the worry, the grudge. Decide now what you'll do when it shows up, and what you'll do with the hour instead.
Then rest in the quiet. This hour won't come twice.

wordCard.voice: Memento mori. Latin for remember you will die: not to frighten you, but to sort what matters.

orig.note: Latin: remember that you will die. in some art, shown as a skull.

carryVoice: Keep this one: remember, and live, because the end shows you what the hour is for. See you tomorrow.
